Thank you for submitting your article "Corticostriatal deficit introduces temporal limits to automatic action in aging" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom, Geoffrey Schoenbaum (Reviewer#1), is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Richard Ivry as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

In this study the authors tested the ability of young and aged mice to organize actions in an RR20 lever pressing task into discrete sequences or chunks. Young controls developed lever press sequences that were of the approximate correct length to obtain reward efficiently, with short periods between presses, and longer periods preceding the first press after a magazine entry or following the last press before entry. Aged mice also increased their pressing, however their behavior was more sporadic. Sequences were shorter, executed much more quickly, and gaps between presses and other presses and between presses and food magazine behavior were not distinguishable. As a result, aged mice were much less efficient at harvesting reward. The authors use MAPK expression to identify a circuit including mPFC and dorsal striatum normally involved in habit learning in which activity seemed to be reduced in aged subjects. Cuing aged rats with a tone at the end of the sequences allowed for temporary rescue of their behavior, indicating changes were not low level motor problems. But improved performance was not lasting if the cue was removed. Chemogenetic inactivation of direct pathway neurons in young controls in dorsolateral striatum reproduced some of the speeding and microchunking behavior but did not affect overall efficiency the same way.

Essential revisions:

The reviewers identified 3 areas that required revisions that were deemed essential for publication. The first and most important is to clarify that the behavior shown by young rats is in fact chunked and that this is lost in aged rats. While the current detailed analysis was appreciated by all 3 reviewers, it lacks some of the traditional measures to show this. This is captured most clearly by the comment by reviewer 2 on sequence variability in Figure 1 and also analysis of Figure 3. The second critical area was to address whether the deficit shown is primarily in sequence generation or whether this is secondary to another problem, such as inability to hear the pellet dispenser or differences in the use of the trigger in the sequence in aged rats or perhaps simply locomotor problems. Finally there were concerns about the dose of CNO used and also generally the differences between the pattern of effect of the deficit in this experiment versus what is shown by the aged rats. These must all be addressed to satisfy the reviewers.

Reviewer #1:

In this study the authors tested the ability of young and aged mice to organize actions in a simple lever pressing task in to discrete sequences or chunks. Mice were trained on a RR20 task in which chunking was encouraged by a requirement that a series of presses be executed without checking the magazine in order to "access" the RR20 sequence. In young controls, this resulted in the development of lever press sequences that were of the approximate correct length, with short periods between presses, and longer periods preceding the first press after a magazine entry or following the last press before entry. Aged mice also increased their pressing, however their behavior was more sporadic. Sequences were shorter, executed much more quickly, and gaps between presses and other presses and between presses and food magazine behavior were not distinguishable. As a result, aged mice were much less efficient at harvesting reward. The authors use MAPK expression to identify a circuit including mPFC and dorsal striatum normally involved in habit learning in which activity seemed to be reduced in aged subjects. Cuing aged rats with a tone at the end of the sequences allowed for temporary rescue of their behavior, indicating changes were not low level motor problems. But improved performance was not lasting if the cue was removed. Chemogenetic inactivation of direct pathway neurons in young controls in dorsolateral striatum reproduced some of the speeding and microchunking behavior but did not affect overall efficiency the same way.

Overall the study is excellent. It addresses a very interesting question of how action chunking is affected by aging with an elegant and carefully designed and analyzed task. The authors use gene expression to link changes in aged mice with alterations in a neural circuit implicated by a number of labs in the motor sequence learning, and they go the extra mile to manipulate an important part of this circuit to reproduce part of the deficit which gives confidence that the deficits are related to the genetic markers of function. I only have a few suggestions.

One question I had is whether there is any relationship between the aged rats behavior and the unusual requirement for a short burst of presses to access the RR20 routine. I am not sure I understand fully what this means and its implications, but it seemed to me initially that the microchunks could be influenced by this unusual requirement. Is there any possibility of this?

Second I think the authors need to do a better job clarifying the relationship they see between the aging deficit and the effects of the chemogenetic manipulation. It reproduced some features of the aged mice, but it did not cause the loss of efficiency or (oddly) the pattern of IPI's between lever presses versus magazine-lever interactions (panels K). This seems like it deserves to be noted more clearly in the results (assuming I am not misunderstanding) and hit more head on in the discussion. Obviously there is no reason to require one specific pathway to account for all the changes in aging. Just saying this more clearly would be helpful, unless there is a more specific or different explanation.

Lastly I think the authors should make clearer in the discussion why one would think the microchunking in the aged mice is a form of habit or model-free learning. They discuss nicely why their data suggests it is not. But there was not much of a lead in to this section to convince me this was an important question.

Reviewer #2:

This is an interesting body of work examining the capacity for sequence generation in aged mice. A self-initiated paradigm is employed (minus Figure 6) to examine the generation of sequences in lever press behavior devoid of any obvious predictive cue. They report decreased capacity of aged mice to develop automatic sequences, and proceed to investigate circuit activation, potential contribution, and rescue. While there are some nice behavioral analyses, it is not clear that mice are producing automatic sequences; there is a noted absence of analyses on the variability in any aspect of sequence generation. There are major concerns about the circuit activity analyses, and the targeted circuit manipulation was a blunt measure of direct pathway involvement and does not provide any insight into how D1 SPNs may differentially encode or represent sequences. In addition, there are interpretational concerns that arise with the data from the rescue experiment. Overall, while the data approach was interesting, it largely appears that older mice might just be checking more, or at least aging predisposes an increase in checking behaviors. At this point, the conclusion that aging results in impairments specifically to sequence generation in aged mice and related deficits in associated neurobiological mechanisms is not all together convincing.

Concerns

Figure 1: In relation to Figure 1, necessary data and analyses for interpretation are missing. Do young and old mice differ on the amount of sequences performed? Data should be included on how well mice were able to meet the sequence trigger (the efficiency graph on Figure 3D addresses overall performance, but not performance of the ST). It is possible that the aged mice never learned the contingency between the ST and access to the RR, particularly as age is known to engender behavioral inflexibility, and pre-training without the ST requirement may have prevented its acquisition. It would similarly be of interest to examine sequence behavior in these two groups prior to the introduction of the ST requirement.

In addition, the authors should include analysis and discussion of how variable their sequence behavior is. In Figure 1F it appears as though, even by day 17 of training, there is substantial variability associated with the sequences length and duration, both within and across subjects. To what extent are the mice actually performing stereotyped sequences vs. variable ones? This is an important concern, since automaticity would be expected to lead to relatively invariable sequences, yet it appears as though the sequences are highly variable, and therefore, it is unclear how mice are understanding and solving the task.

Also missing are appropriate post hoc analyses that would arise from the significant interactions reported for D and E, which may affect the conclusions proposed. For example, a significant interaction is reported for Figure 1D, and indeed the magnitude of sequence length is visually different between young and aged. However, all additional follow up analyses were not performed. They report a main factor of day for both young and old, but no comparison is made between young and aged for the different days. It seems likely that a difference would arise between ages on Day 17. This could then raise an additional hypothesis that aged mice do not extend sequences in the same manner, and importantly, and such, changes in the variability of such sequences needs to be examined.

Figure 3: The chunking analyses are quite interesting, however, they rely on visual interpretation of differences. The authors should apply some quantitative methods to these data to assess group differences. For instance, visually (figure supplement) it appears as though aged mice simply perform many more sequences than young mice (see concern above about amount of sequences), which might explain some of the chunking results. Proportional analyses may be appropriate here. As it stands, this data does not provide evidence that aged and young animals chunk sequences differently (and may suggest different amounts of overall lever pressing). Average inter-event intervals of various types could also be compared and would be informative.

Figure 4: The investigation into how recruitment of activity in corticostriatal networks represented in Figure 4 is somewhat troubling, in that it may be inherently confounded by general differences in lever pressing and have nothing to do with sequence generation. Are the groups matched for total lever presses? Is it that one group (aged) is just making more lever presses and hence, that could account for the differential activation in the circuit (based on action execution and nothing to do with sequence generation)? In Figure 4C, the large variability between subjects is apparent, and while various sequence factors were correlated with counts observed, whether overall lever presses correlated was not presented. Given this variability within a given group, do similar relationships arise for within group correlations? Further, for the analyses in D and E, how is the variability in each animal factor into the variability in the overall analyses? This is not clear in the Materials and methods. Are total activity levels normalized is some manner?

Figure 5: The CNO dosage used is quite high (3mg/kg), and this coupled with repeated dosing across days raises concerns about the potential changes in plasticity that may have occurred. This would raise alternative hypotheses other than an effect of altered D1 SPNs underlying sequence deficits in older animals. If specifically, D1 SPNs control over sequence execution is altered in aged mice, then acute attenuation should result in some alteration in performance. Also, it is unclear from the present data if dMSNs in the DLS are important in learning/acquiring these sequences, in their performance, or both. Although not unconvincing, for Figure 5I and J, the authors should have consistency between the data presented here and in Figure 3B and C. In Figure 3, the authors show IPI and speed data from only the fastest sequences, while in Figure 5 the speed and IPI data appears to be collapsed across all sequences. Does CNO replicate the effect on the fastest sequences, and additionally, does age have the same overall effect as CNO appears to? Is there any effect on the overall number of sequences? Why was the comparison made at day 10 instead of 7 (different schedule requirements were in place)? Perhaps the authors should temper their comparisons between age and dMSN inhibition. Particularly since CNO did not recapitulate the effects of age on either action chunking or task performance (where indeed, CNO and age had opposite effects).

Figure 6: This is interesting data, but also seems open to additional interpretations. While the introduction of the auditory cue could be perceived as action feedback, it may also act as a conditioned reinforcer and able to support actions independently. The authors raise the spectrum of cognitive as well as motor deficits in aging, but initiating actions under the control of conditioned reinforcement is a different hypothesis than self-initiated automatic action sequences. Additionally, the improved performance in aged mice with the addition of a loud salient auditory noise also raises the question of what action feedback is missing in Figure 1? Old mice in these age ranges, especially C57s loose large frequencies ranges in their hearing capacity. They appear to hear the white noise, but it does raise the potential that they are missing some other auditory cue that is there during sequence learning. Are they just hearing impaired and can't rely on any auditory feedback that normally arises during training (pellet dropping, lever, etc.)? This may not reflect anything on the ability to form sequences exactly, but to use auditory information?

Reviewer #3:

These data show action sequence chunking in young mice that is disrupted in aged mice. Aged mice show shorter action sequences that are, somewhat unexpectedly, sped up. This is associated with disrupted activation of caudolateral corticostriatal networks and is restored with the addition of a sequence termination feedback stimulus. Selective inactivation of DLS D1-expressing MSNs, like aging, also caused increased sequence speed. The behavioral analysis is novel and strong and is itself a significant contribution to the field. I particularly appreciate the inclusion of individual data. The ability to remedy the behavioral deficit with the feedback cue in aged mice is also a major strength of the report. The report is well-written and likely to make a significant contribution to several fields.

1) It is not clear how the DLS D1-MSN inactivation data relate to the aging data. Both findings are very interesting in their own right. But the manuscript (e.g., these statements from the Abstract: "Pharmacogenetic disruption of a striatal subcircuit in young mice reproduced most age-related action features" and Results "we hypothesized that age-related changes in corticostriatal function and resulting hypoactivity of dSPNs in the DLS could be generating deficits in action sequence latencies. We directly tested this possibility […]") implies that disrupted DLS D1 MSN activity underlies the deficits in aged mice. There are no data to support this and the DLS D1 MSN inactivation does not recapitulate the full or even most of the phenotype of aged mice. Gathering data to link these two data sets (e.g., evaluation of DLS D1 MSN activity in aged mice), as far as I can tell, is not feasible on any sort of reasonable timeframe. One option is to remove these data from the report. If they are included, then their presentation should be changed throughout to make clear this is not an evaluation of the mechanism of the aging effect and the limitations linking this result to the aging result should be thoroughly discussed.

2) Is it possible that differences in the ability to hear explain the differences in sequence performance in young vs. aged mice? The click of the pellet dispense provides a subtle cue signaling reward delivery. If the aged mice cannot hear this, they cannot use it as a cue to signal they should terminate pressing and check the magazine, as a result they have shorted sequences because they have to check the magazine more often. Data to support or refute this possibility are needed. Perhaps there are data from the literature to draw on. This possibility might also explain why the explicit auditory feedback cue that the aged mice can hear facilitates sequence duration in the aged mice.

3) Related to point 2, inspection of Figure 1F indicates that aged mice are checking the magazine more than the young mice. These data should be included and the possibility that the altered sequence performance is secondary to altered reward checking behavior should be discussed.

4) What is the rationale for analyzing only the 5 fastest sequences for the main data (Figure 3B,C), but all sequences for the D1-MSN inactivation data (Figure I, J)? It would be preferable to analyze the sequence speed and IPI comparison for all sequences for both data sets.

5) Please include a quantification and statistical comparison of p-MAPK following CNO/GBR12783 on the hM4Di expressing v. non-expressing hemisphere, or inside v. outside the hM4di-mCherry expression zones.

6) Please include individual data as in Figure 1F for the DLS D1 MSN inactivation data presented in Figure 5.

results.result: Aged mice produce shorter, more frequent action sequences compared to young mice. After extended training, aged mice displayed sequences that could be extended in number of elements but not temporally sustained, with significantly shorter durations than young mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C26-C31, C35-C36, and C41 provide converging behavioral evidence from multiple measures (sequence frequency, length, duration) with appropriate statistical tests showing significant training x age interactions. The data consistently demonstrate that aged mice develop qualitatively different sequence structures.

results.result: Aged mice show temporal constraints in sustained action performance. In lever hold tasks, aged mice maintained maximum performance around 0.5 seconds while young mice continued to increase hold times, suggesting action sequences in aged mice are influenced by temporal constraints.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C51 present consistent behavioral data from lever hold experiments with appropriate statistical analyses (mixed ANOVA, simple effects). The convergence of timestamp and visual data (event scatter plots, event-time diagrams) provides strong support for temporal constraints in aged mice.

results.result: Aged mice display ultrafast action sequences with speeds exceeding 13 presses per second, similar to automatized reflex movements. Despite this speed, aged mice were less efficient at earning rewards.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 and C74 are supported by both timestamp and acoustic analysis data. The use of acoustic methods to overcome temporal resolution limits (C53, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) strengthens the findings. Statistical comparisons confirm significantly higher speeds and shorter inter-press-intervals in aged mice.

results.result: Aged mice show aberrant motor chunking characterized by ultrafast within-sequence chunking and early chunking of sequence boundary elements. Young mice chunk only within-sequence elements with longer boundary intervals, while aged mice accumulate boundary intervals in a narrow band near the chunking space appearing as early as day 10.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C77 present detailed temporal analysis of inter-press-intervals with appropriate statistical tests showing differential chunking patterns. The visual representations (Figure 3G-K) combined with quantitative analyses of interval distributions, variability, and timing provide strong converging evidence for distinct automaticity processes in aged mice.

results.result: Aged mice show deficient reorganization of corticostriatal activity during action sequence execution, with reduced activation in dorsolateral striatum (DLS) and frontoparietal cortex (FPx). These regions uniquely predicted sequence features, and aged mice showed widespread correlations in rostromedial but not caudolateral territories.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C94 present extensive neuronal mapping data (>60,000 neurons) with appropriate statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA, simple effects, correlation analyses). The p-MAPK mapping methodology is well-established (C81). The convergence of activation patterns, correlation analyses, and spatial mapping provides strong support for age-related corticostriatal deficits.

results.result: Chemogenetic inhibition of direct pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs) in dorsolateral striatum of young mice reproduced within-sequence features of aged behavior (shorter durations, higher speeds, shorter inter-press-intervals) but not extra-sequence features (boundary intervals remained normal).
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C121 present well-controlled chemogenetic experiments with validation of viral specificity and functional inhibition (C101-C103). Statistical analyses appropriately compare dSPN-hM4Di(+) and control mice across multiple behavioral measures. The partial recapitulation of aged phenotype (within-sequence but not boundary features) is clearly demonstrated and appropriately interpreted (C120).

results.result: Action-related feedback cues temporarily restore normal sequence structure in aged mice. Upon cue removal, sequence length and duration dropped to pre-sequence levels, and microchunks were instantly precipitated, suggesting the deficit is cognitive-motor rather than purely executional.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C139 present a well-designed intervention experiment with appropriate controls (Cue Maintained vs. Cue Lost groups). Statistical analyses (mixed ANOVA, simple effects) demonstrate significant effects of cue removal. The temporal dynamics of sequence degradation within a session (C130-C133) and the instant precipitation of microchunks (C137) provide strong evidence for the cognitive-motor nature of the deficit.

results.result: Control experiments demonstrate that aged mice can detect pellet delivery through vibration signals and show similar learning of magazine approach responses as young mice, ruling out sensory deficits as an explanation for behavioral differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 present appropriate control experiments with acoustic/vibration measurements and behavioral analyses. Statistical tests show no training x age interaction in magazine training, confirming that sensory detection is intact in aged mice. This strengthens the interpretation that observed deficits reflect motor sequence learning rather than sensory impairments.

results.result: Overall instrumental performance (lever press rate) was equal in young and aged mice throughout training, with both groups significantly escalating performance as ratio requirements increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by appropriate mixed ANOVA showing significant main effect of training but no training x age interaction. This establishes that general learning capacity and motivation are intact in aged mice, providing important context for interpreting sequence-specific deficits.

results.result: Aged mice showed evidence of learning about the sequence trigger requirement by frequently breaking through it to access the random ratio schedule, while young mice kept breakthrough numbers low.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis showing significant training x age interaction. This demonstrates that aged mice learned the task contingencies but implemented them differently, consistent with the microchunking interpretation.

results.result: Ultrafast action chunks in aged mice correlated with deficient reorganization of corticostriatal activity. Specifically, sequence features (length, duration, speed) were predicted only by activation in DLS and FPx, with shorter/faster sequences predicting lower DLS activity in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C87, and C157 present correlation analyses linking behavioral and neuronal measures. The specificity of DLS/FPx correlations (C87) and the direction of effects in aged mice (C157) are clearly demonstrated. However, correlational data cannot establish causation, which is appropriately addressed through the chemogenetic experiments.

results.result: Chemogenetic disruption of dSPNs in DLS reproduced aspects of aged behavior and demonstrated that reducing dSPN activity decreases action duration while increasing speed, supporting and extending findings on dSPN involvement in encoding action latency.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C158, C178-C179 integrate the chemogenetic findings with prior literature. The results are consistent with cited work on dSPN function (Jin et al., 2014; Tecuapetla et al., 2016) while extending understanding to aging. The partial recapitulation appropriately acknowledges limitations.

results.result: Introduction of action-related feedback cues temporarily restored normal sequence structure in aged mice, and this intervention could be implemented in rehabilitation strategies for cognitive aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C189 are supported by the feedback cue experiment data. The temporary restoration is clearly demonstrated (C125-C128), and the suggestion for clinical application (C190) is appropriately framed as a possibility supported by citation to relevant human literature (Lindenberger and Mayr, 2014).

results.result: Static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks introduce temporal limits to action automaticity that compromise procedural learning. The stationarity of cortico-basal ganglia transmission is a major feature hampering skill acquisition in aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C185-C186, and C188 represent the main conclusions integrating behavioral and neuronal findings. These are well-supported by the convergence of evidence from multiple experiments showing temporal constraints (C42-C51), aberrant chunking (C59-C77), deficient neural reorganization (C80-C94), and partial rescue by feedback (C124-C139).

results.result: Age-related hypoactivation of dSPNs in the DLS could be contributing to deficits in action sequence learning observed in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 represents a hypothesis that is subsequently tested through chemogenetic experiments. The hypothesis is reasonable based on the p-MAPK mapping data (C92, C94) and prior literature on dSPN function (C97-C99). The chemogenetic results (C101-C121) provide partial support, showing that dSPN inhibition reproduces within-sequence but not all features of aging.

results.result: Older subjects (mice and humans) consistently develop a form of chunking involving shorter and faster sequences (microchunks), suggesting that automation of actions is possible in aging but is temporally distorted compared to younger individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 integrate the current mouse findings with human literature (Bo et al., 2009). The comparison is appropriate given similar patterns across species, though differences between homogeneous and heterogeneous sequence learning are acknowledged (C142). The conclusion about temporal distortion is well-supported by the combined evidence.

results.result: Neuronal activity assessments suggest aged brains fail to disengage rostro-medial corticostriatal circuits, and the predicted medial-to-lateral shifts during automatic behavior development may not occur or only occur partially. This neuronal staticity might explain recruitment of unusual automaticity processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C156, C165-C166 are supported by the p-MAPK mapping data showing widespread correlations in rostromedial territories (C90-C91) and reduced activation in caudolateral regions (C92) in aged mice. This contrasts with the expected pattern based on established models of habit formation (C78-C79, C151), providing novel insight into aging effects.

results.result: The execution of microchunks is not a consequence of deficient learning but rather reflects different automaticity processes. Young and aged brains start from different neuronal environments and implement entirely different strategies for automaticity to optimize task performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C164 represent key interpretive conclusions supported by the feedback cue experiment showing that aged mice can execute long sequences with appropriate cues (C160-C161) and instantly revert to microchunks upon cue removal (C137). This demonstrates intact learning capacity but different automaticity implementation, consistent with the scaffolding framework (Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009).

results.result: Multiple speculative mechanisms are proposed to explain microchunking in aging, including automaticity-related reductions in neuronal variability, loss of action-related feedback, working memory limitations driving early model-free processing, compensatory prefrontal overactivation, and temporal scaling constraints.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C122, C150, C155, C166, C169-C170, C173, C175-C176, and C183 represent speculative interpretations appropriately labeled as such in the text. While these hypotheses are reasonable and grounded in cited literature, they are not directly tested in the current study. The speculation is appropriate for a Discussion section but should not be considered established findings.

results.result: Background claims establish the theoretical framework including motor skill acquisition principles, motor chunking concepts, cortico-basal ganglia circuit organization, age-related motor learning deficits in humans, computational advantages of model-free behavior, and prior findings on dSPN function and temporal processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C21, C78-C79, C81, C95-C99, C140-C142, C146-C149, C151-C154, C167-C168, C172, C174, C177, C180-C181 represent established knowledge appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings but are not original contributions of this study.

results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are straightforward methodological details clearly stated in the text. The age selection is appropriate for studying aging effects in mice (average life expectancy 24 months noted in Discussion).

results.result: The chemogenetic striatal manipulations did not recreate accompanying prefronto-parietal dysfunction and resulting working memory deficits present in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C182 appropriately acknowledges a limitation of the chemogenetic approach. This is an important caveat for interpreting why young mice with dSPN inhibition showed increased rather than decreased reward efficiency (C121, C183), unlike aged mice (C58).

results.result: On day 7, both groups showed no sequence structure, but by day 17, both young and aged mice developed clearly defined action sequences with identifiable initiation, execution, and termination elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by visual analysis of event-time plots. This establishes that both groups successfully learned to form sequences, providing important baseline for comparing sequence quality and structure between groups.

results.result: Peak speeds within fast sequence bursts in dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice were not as high as those recorded in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 notes an important difference between the chemogenetic model and natural aging. This is consistent with the interpretation that dSPN inhibition reproduces only some features of aging (C120) and supports the conclusion that multiple mechanisms contribute to the aged phenotype.

results.result: The results add to studies elucidating the microcircuitry responsible for the temporal scaling of action.
results.evaluation: Claim C184 appropriately positions the findings within the broader literature on temporal processing in motor control. The chemogenetic results (C178) provide novel evidence for dSPN involvement in action duration that complements prior optogenetic studies (C180-C181).

results.result: Aged mice produced shorter action sequences compared to young mice after extended training. While both groups could extend sequences in terms of number of elements, aged mice produced more frequent but temporally shorter sequences that could not be sustained over time like those of young mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises critical concerns about whether the behavior represents true chunking versus simply increased checking behavior, noting 'it is not clear that mice are producing automatic sequences' and requesting 'analysis and discussion of how variable their sequence behavior is.' Reviewer 2 also questions whether 'older mice might just be checking more' and requests data on sequence variability and stereotypy. Reviewer 3 notes that 'inspection of Figure 1F indicates that aged mice are checking the magazine more than the young mice' and requests these data be included with discussion of whether altered sequence performance is secondary to altered reward checking.

results.result: Aged mice displayed ultrafast action sequences with very short inter-press intervals, producing 'microchunks' with speeds over 13 presses per second. These ultrafast sequences showed early chunking of boundary elements and were less efficient at earning rewards despite their speed.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The chunking analyses are quite interesting, however, they rely on visual interpretation of differences' and requests 'some quantitative methods to these data to assess group differences.' Reviewer 2 notes that 'visually it appears as though aged mice simply perform many more sequences than young mice' and suggests 'Proportional analyses may be appropriate here.' The reviewer concludes 'this data does not provide evidence that aged and young animals chunk sequences differently (and may suggest different amounts of overall lever pressing).' Reviewer 1 asks for clarification on whether microchunks could be influenced by the unusual sequence trigger requirement.

results.result: p-MAPK mapping revealed age-related deficits in posterior corticostriatal networks, with reduced activation in dorsolateral striatum (DLS) and frontoparietal cortex (FPx) in aged mice. Aged mice showed widespread correlations in rostromedial but not caudolateral territories, and sequence features correlated only with DLS and FPx activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises major concerns that the circuit activity analysis 'may be inherently confounded by general differences in lever pressing and have nothing to do with sequence generation.' The reviewer asks 'Are the groups matched for total lever presses? Is it that one group (aged) is just making more lever presses and hence, that could account for the differential activation in the circuit (based on action execution and nothing to do with sequence generation)?' Reviewer 2 also questions how variability in each animal factors into the analyses and whether 'total activity levels normalized is some manner.' These methodological concerns undermine confidence in the neural circuit conclusions.

results.result: Chemogenetic disruption of dSPNs in the DLS of young mice reproduced some age-related features including increased sequence speed and shorter within-sequence intervals, but did not affect sequence boundary intervals or reduce reward efficiency like aging did.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers express concerns about the relationship between chemogenetic manipulation and aging effects. Reviewer 1 states the manipulation 'reproduced some features of the aged mice, but it did not cause the loss of efficiency or (oddly) the pattern of IPI's between lever presses versus magazine-lever interactions' and requests this be 'noted more clearly in the results' and 'hit more head on in the discussion.' Reviewer 3 states 'the DLS D1 MSN inactivation does not recapitulate the full or even most of the phenotype of aged mice' and notes the manuscript 'implies that disrupted DLS D1 MSN activity underlies the deficits in aged mice. There are no data to support this.' Reviewer 2 raises concerns about the high CNO dose (3mg/kg) with repeated dosing and notes 'CNO did not recapitulate the effects of age on either action chunking or task performance (where indeed, CNO and age had opposite effects).' Reviewer 2 also questions inconsistencies in data presentation between Figure 3 and Figure 5.

results.result: Introduction of an action-related auditory feedback cue temporarily restored normal sequence structure in aged mice. When the cue was removed, sequences rapidly shortened back to microchunks, suggesting the deficit is cognitive-motor rather than purely executional.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant interpretational concerns, noting 'the introduction of the auditory cue could be perceived as action feedback, it may also act as a conditioned reinforcer and able to support actions independently.' The reviewer states 'initiating actions under the control of conditioned reinforcement is a different hypothesis than self-initiated automatic action sequences.' Reviewer 2 and Reviewer 3 both raise the critical concern about hearing impairment: 'Old mice in these age ranges, especially C57s loose large frequencies ranges in their hearing capacity' and ask 'Are they just hearing impaired and can't rely on any auditory feedback that normally arises during training (pellet dropping, lever, etc.)?' Reviewer 3 specifically asks 'Is it possible that differences in the ability to hear explain the differences in sequence performance in young vs. aged mice?' and requests 'Data to support or refute this possibility are needed.'

results.result: Aged mice showed evidence of learning about the sequence trigger requirement and magazine training, with similar reductions in reaction times and increases in magazine approach responses as young mice. However, aged mice produced more sequences that broke through the sequence trigger compared to young mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests data on 'how well mice were able to meet the sequence trigger' noting 'It is possible that the aged mice never learned the contingency between the ST and access to the RR.' The manuscript provides statistical evidence that aged mice did learn the sequence trigger (showing marked increases in sequences breaking through the ST), though they used it differently than young mice. The magazine training data showing equivalent learning across age groups is not directly challenged by reviewers.

results.result: In a lever hold task, both young and aged mice increased hold times up to ~0.5 seconds, but only young mice continued to increase beyond this point. Aged mice maintained maximum performance around 0.5 seconds, suggesting temporal constraints on action sequences.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes the overall study as 'excellent' and states 'It addresses a very interesting question of how action chunking is affected by aging with an elegant and carefully designed and analyzed task.' The lever hold data is not specifically challenged by any reviewer and provides converging evidence for temporal constraints. Reviewer 3 notes 'The behavioral analysis is novel and strong and is itself a significant contribution to the field.'

results.result: Both young and aged mice significantly escalated their overall lever press performance as training progressed, with no significant difference in overall instrumental performance between age groups, though there was a significant interaction in the number of sequences produced per minute.
results.evaluation: This basic behavioral finding is not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes the study uses 'an elegant and carefully designed and analyzed task' and Reviewer 3 states 'The behavioral analysis is novel and strong.' The concern raised is about interpretation of what this performance represents (chunking vs. checking behavior) rather than the data itself.

results.result: The study concludes that static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks introduce temporal limits to action automaticity, compromising procedural learning. The aged brain implements different automaticity strategies rather than simply failing to learn, starting from a different neuronal scaffolding.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 requests the authors 'make clearer in the discussion why one would think the microchunking in the aged mice is a form of habit or model-free learning' noting 'there was not much of a lead in to this section to convince me this was an important question.' The interpretation that aged mice use different strategies is questioned by Reviewer 2's concerns about whether the behavior represents true automaticity versus increased checking. Reviewer 3's concern about hearing impairment potentially explaining the results also challenges this interpretation. The conclusion about 'static properties' of networks is undermined by Reviewer 2's methodological concerns about the circuit activity analyses.

comparisons.comparison: Both address behavioral evidence for sequence structure differences (C3, C4, C26, C28-C31, C35-C36, C41). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with converging measures and appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising critical concerns about whether behavior represents true chunking versus increased checking behavior, requesting analysis of sequence variability and stereotypy.

Both evaluate lever hold experiment data (C42-C51). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with consistent behavioral data and appropriate statistical analyses demonstrating temporal constraints. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 describing the study as 'excellent' and Reviewer 3 noting 'behavioral analysis is novel and strong.' No specific challenges to these claims.

Both address speed and inter-press-interval findings (C52-C58, C74). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by timestamp and acoustic data with statistical confirmation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting chunking analyses 'rely on visual interpretation' and requesting 'quantitative methods to assess group differences' and proportional analyses, concluding data may not provide evidence of different chunking.

Both evaluate detailed temporal analysis of inter-press-intervals and chunking patterns (C59-C77). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong converging evidence from visual and quantitative analyses. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating analyses 'rely on visual interpretation' and that 'aged mice simply perform many more sequences,' suggesting proportional analyses may be needed and questioning whether groups differ in chunking versus overall lever pressing.

Both address neuronal mapping and p-MAPK data (C80-C94). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with extensive data and appropriate statistical analyses showing age-related corticostriatal deficits. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising major concerns that circuit activity 'may be inherently confounded by general differences in lever pressing' and questioning whether groups are matched for total lever presses, undermining confidence in neural circuit conclusions.

Both evaluate chemogenetic experiments (C101-C121). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting well-controlled experiments with appropriate validation and interpretation of partial recapitulation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with all three reviewers expressing concerns that manipulation 'reproduced some features' but 'did not recapitulate the full or even most of the phenotype,' questioning high CNO dose, noting inconsistencies in data presentation, and stating 'There are no data to support' that disrupted dSPN activity underlies aged deficits.

Both address feedback cue intervention experiment (C124-C139). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with well-designed experiment and appropriate controls demonstrating cognitive-motor nature of deficit. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns that auditory cue 'may also act as a conditioned reinforcer' (different hypothesis), and critically questioning whether aged C57 mice have hearing impairment that could explain all differences in sequence performance.

Both evaluate control experiments on sensory detection (C37-C40) and sequence trigger learning (C32-C33). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, confirming sensory detection intact and that aged mice learned contingencies. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, though Reviewer 2 requests additional data on how well mice met sequence trigger. The magazine training data showing equivalent learning is not directly challenged.

Both address general learning capacity and motivation (C24-C25). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate mixed ANOVA showing intact general learning. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, with no specific challenges to this basic behavioral finding. Reviewers note the task is 'elegant and carefully designed' and 'behavioral analysis is novel and strong.'

Both address sequence trigger learning (C32-C33). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED showing aged mice learned contingencies but implemented differently. Peer reviewers find SUPPORTED, though Reviewer 2 requests additional data on how well mice met the sequence trigger, noting 'It is possible that the aged mice never learned the contingency.'

Both address correlation analyses linking behavioral and neuronal measures (C5, C87, C157). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment that correlation cannot establish causation. Peer reviewers rate the broader neural circuit analysis UNCERTAIN due to methodological concerns about confounding by general lever pressing differences.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with concerns that the manuscript 'implies that disrupted DLS D1 MSN activity underlies the deficits in aged mice. There are no data to support this.'

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about hearing impairment in aged C57 mice potentially explaining results and questioning whether auditory cue acts as conditioned reinforcer rather than action feedback.
